# Web Content Accessibility Guidelines

## Summary

The English Wikipedia article on WCAG, the accessibility recommendations published by the Web Accessibility Initiative of the W3C. The lead explains that they aim to make web content accessible mainly to people with disabilities, and also to limited devices such as phones. It gives the main milestones: WCAG 2.0 in December 2008, adopted as an ISO/IEC standard in 2012, and WCAG 2.2 as a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. The body covers the structure of the guidelines (principles, guidelines, testable success criteria at levels A, AA and AAA), the differences between versions, and how laws and procurement rules in various places refer to them.

## Why It Matters

WCAG is the standard behind every audit I sell and every accessibility argument I make with clients. I read this article in the first week of the Sablewing course ([[accessibility-deep-dive-2025]]) to get the history straight before the course went into success criteria one by one; I had been saying "WCAG 2.1" to clients long after 2.2 existed.

Where it shows up in my work:

- The [[thistlewood-catalog-audit]] was scoped as WCAG 2.2 AA, and my [[wcag-audit-checklist]] follows the 2.2 success criteria.
- The Copperline two-teal decision ([[copperline-accessibility-review-2026-02-11]]) rests on the contrast minimum for text (4.5:1) and the lower 3:1 threshold for large text and interface components. Brand teal #2BA59F reaches 3.0:1 on white, enough for decoration and large headings but not for body text or button labels; text teal #0F766E reaches 5.5:1. The reasoning is in [[color-contrast-for-text]].
- Copperline's project outcome names WCAG 2.2 AA as a target ([[copperline-online-banking-redesign]]), and the [[tallowmere-ticketing-audit]] uses the same level.
- Lintel Kit V2's contrast-checked color pairs follow the same thresholds.

## Key Details

- Three conformance levels; AA is what clients, procurement documents and most laws ask for.
- Success criteria are meant to be testable, which is what makes an audit report defensible: each finding cites one.
- WCAG 2.2 added criteria relevant to my work, such as target size and focus not being obscured.

## Caveats

An encyclopedia overview, not the standard. For an audit I cite the W3C text and its Understanding documents, not Wikipedia. The legal sections vary by country and I never rely on them; legal obligations are for the client's own counsel. Passing AA does not make a site usable for disabled people; it is a floor, which is why every audit also includes [[screen-reader-testing]].
